claim: Rouget first discovered pericytes in 1873 and observed that these cells might serve as contractile entities to regulate microcirculatory blood flow because of their structure and position on microvessels.
source: When Rouget first discovered pericytes in 1873, he observed that these cells might serve as contractile entities to regulate microcirculatory blood flow because of their structure and position on microvessels (Rouget, 1873).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rouget's 1873 work.

claim: Microcirculatory blood flow is largely regulated by upstream arterioles rich in α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA).
source: However, this idea was later challenged based on findings that microcirculatory blood flow is largely regulated by upstream arterioles rich in α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), the contractile protein present in vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most capillary pericytes in the central nervous system contained little or no α-SMA, whereas α-SMA was detected in pericytes located on pre-capillary arterioles and post-capillary venules.
source: A number of studies in the past three decades reported that most capillary pericytes in the central nervous system contained little or no α-SMA, whereas α-SMA was detected in pericytes located on pre-capillary arterioles and post-capillary venules (Bandopadhyay et al., 2001; Nehls and Drenckhahn, 1991; Kur et al., 2012; Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Armulik et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: A subgroup of capillary pericytes are contractile in the brain and retina, and have the capacity to regulate the microcirculation by contracting and relaxing in response to physiological and pharmacological stimuli.
source: In contrast, recent in vitro and in vivo functional studies have demonstrated that a subgroup of capillary pericytes are contractile in the brain and retina, and have the capacity to regulate the microcirculation by contracting and relaxing in response to physiological (i.e. neurovascular coupling) as well as pharmacological stimuli (Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Hall et al., 2014; Peppiatt et al., 2006; Fernández-Klett et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple functional studies.

claim: Capillaries covered by pericytes dilate before arterioles in response to neuronal stimulus in situ.
source: Importantly, Hall et al. showed that capillaries covered by pericytes dilate before arte-rioles in response to neuronal stimulus in situ (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al. 2014.

claim: An increase in astrocytic calcium mediates brain capillary changes in response to metabolic demand.
source: Recently, an increase in astrocytic calcium was shown to mediate brain capillary changes in response to metabolic demand (Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mishra et al. 2016.

claim: Calcium signaling in Müller cell endfeet is sufficient to evoke capillary dilation in the retina.
source: Similarly, Biesecker et al. showed that calcium signaling in Müller cell endfeet was sufficient to evoke capillary dilation in the retina (Biesecker et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Biesecker et al. 2016.

claim: Transgenic mice with a decreased number of pericytes had deficient neurovascular coupling and reduced oxygen delivery to the brain.
source: Kisler et al. reported that transgenic mice with a decreased number of pericytes had deficient neurovascular coupling and reduced oxygen delivery to the brain (Kisler et al., 2017), providing additional evidence for the importance of pericytes in blood flow regulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kisler et al. 2017.

claim: α-SMA-expressing pericytes have been redefined as smooth muscle cells by Hill et al. 2015.
source: However, a recent paper dismisses the idea of pericytes being contractile by redefining α-SMA-expressing pericytes as smooth muscle cells (Hill et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hill et al. 2015.

claim: Small amounts of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may be rapidly depolymerized during transcardial perfusion and fixation thus evading detection by immunolabeling.
source: To address this paradox between functional and histological findings, we hypothesized that small amounts of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may be rapidly depolymerized during transcardial perfusion and fixation thus evading detection by immunolabeling.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis that they test in the study.

claim: α-SMA in pericytes has been detected by electron microscopy in which small amounts of α-SMA can be identified.
source: Consistent with this idea, α-SMA in pericytes has been detected by electron microscopy in which small amounts of α-SMA can be identified (Toribatake et al., 1997; Le Beux and Willemot, 1978; Ho, 1985; Nakano et al., 2000) or by in vitro studies in which fixation is more rapidly achieved (Herman and D'Amore, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: When filamentous-actin (F-actin) depolymerization was prevented by F-actin stabilizing agents or by snap fixation, α-SMA was detected in a much larger fraction of microvascular pericytes, including capillary pericytes placed on the intermediate and deeper retinal vascular beds.
source: Here, we show that when filamentous-actin (F-actin) depolymerization was prevented by F-actin stabilizing agents or by snap fixation, we detected α-SMA in a much larger fraction of microvascular pericytes, including capillary pericytes placed on the intermediate and deeper retinal vascular beds.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Substantial F-actin was found in pericyte processes surrounding capillaries.
source: Intriguingly, we found substantial F-actin in pericyte processes surrounding capillaries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Snap freeze fixation of retinas with methanol at −20°C yielded almost twice as many α-SMA-immunopositive microvessels compared to paraformaldehyde (PFA) fixation.
source: Snap freeze fixation of retinas with methanol at −20°C, yielded almost twice as many α-SMA-immunopositive microvessels compared to paraformaldehyde (PFA) fixation (Methanol: 441 ± 28 vessels, PFA: 254 ± 63 vessels, p=0.023; ANOVA) (Supplementary file 1; Figures 1A–B, 2A, C–D and 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The number of α-SMA-labeled microvessels significantly increased in fourth order capillaries with methanol fixation compared to PFA fixation.
source: The number of α-SMA-labeled microvessels significantly increased in fourth order capillaries (Methanol: 144 ± 19 vessels, PFA: 60 ± 28 vessels, p=0.003; ANOVA) (Figures 1A–B, 2A, C–D and 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Ethanol fixation did not improve α-SMA immunostaining.
source: Ethanol fixation did not improve α-SMA immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B), suggesting that the effect of methanol was likely due to a faster fixation and not the result of a nonspecific response (e.g. protein denaturation).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: The effect of methanol on α-SMA detection was likely due to faster fixation and not the result of a nonspecific response.
source: Ethanol fixation did not improve α-SMA immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B), suggesting that the effect of methanol was likely due to a faster fixation and not the result of a nonspecific response (e.g. protein denaturation).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of methanol and ethanol fixation results.

claim: No immunoreactivity was observed in negative controls when the anti-α-SMA primary antibody was omitted.
source: No immunoreactivity was observed in negative controls when the anti-α-SMA primary antibody was omitted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: α-SMA-positive pericytes on capillaries were identified by NG2 or PDGRFβ co-immunolabeling.
source: In addition to their typical bump-on-a-log appearance detected by lectin, the α-SMA-positive pericytes on capillaries were identified by NG2 or PDGRFβ co-immunolabeling (Figure 2B–C), or by their red fluorescence in NG2-DsRed mice, a transgenic line that allows selective visualization of pericytes (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B–D.

claim: NG2-DsRed mice are a transgenic line that allows selective visualization of pericytes.
source: In addition to their typical bump-on-a-log appearance detected by lectin, the α-SMA-positive pericytes on capillaries were identified by NG2 or PDGRFβ co-immunolabeling (Figure 2B–C), or by their red fluorescence in NG2-DsRed mice, a transgenic line that allows selective visualization of pericytes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NG2-DsRed transgenic mouse line.

claim: Most of the γ-actin immunostaining ran longitudinally, parallel to the capillary and pericyte plasma membrane, unlike the circular α-SMA outlining the pericyte somata and processes around the capillaries.
source: Most of the γ-actin immunostaining ran longitudinally, parallel to the capillary and pericyte plasma membrane, unlike the circular α-SMA outlining the pericyte somata and processes around the capillaries (Figure 4A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–G.

claim: γ-actin immunostaining was not detected in pericytes on capillaries after the 4th branch.
source: We did not detect any γ-actin immunostaining in pericytes on capillaries after the 4th branch.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: A redistribution of the immunostaining patterns of γ-actin and α-SMA was not observed when F-actin depolymerization was inhibited with phalloidin.
source: We did not observe a redistribution of the immunostaining patterns of the two actin isoforms when F-actin depolymerization was inhibited with phalloidin (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G.

claim: Phalloidin or jasplakinolide binding to F-actin prevents depolymerization and fixes F-actin in the polymerized state.
source: Phalloidin or jasplakinolide binding to F-actin prevents depolymerization and fixes F-actin in the polymerized state (Auinger and Small, 2008; Cooper, 1987; Lee et al., 2010), thus we reasoned that this strategy might enhance detection of α-SMA in retinal capillary pericytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on phalloidin and jasplakinolide.

claim: Jasplakinolide or phalloidin treatment significantly increased the number of α-SMA-labeling on capillaries of 5th and 6th order compared to PFA fixation.
source: We found that jasplakinolide or phalloidin treatment (Figures 1C, 2B, 3A–D and 5A–C) significantly increased the number of α-SMA-labeling on capillaries of 5th and 6th order compared to PFA fixation (5th order: jasplakinolide = 225 ± 28 vessels, phalloidin = 80 ± 19 vessels, PFA = 15 ± 7 vessels; 6th order: jasplakinolide = 123 ± 30 vessels, phalloidin = 23 ± 9 vessels, PFA = 0 ± 0 vessels, p=0.0001, ANOVA) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Jasplakinolide or phalloidin treatment revealed additional α-SMA-immunolabeling on 7th order capillaries compared to methanol or PFA fixation.
source: Besides this treatment revealed additional α-SMA-immunolabeling on 7th order capillaries (Figures 2B and 5C) compared to methanol or PFA fixation (jasplakinolide: 31 ± 12 vessels, phalloidin: 20 ± 6 vessels, methanol: 0 ± 0 vessels; PFA: 0 ± 0 vessels, p=0.002; ANOVA) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: α-SMA-positive pericytes identified by methanol fixation or phalloidin treatment also expressed NG2 and their number was significantly higher compared to PFA-fixed retinas.
source: α-SMA-positive pericytes identified by methanol fixation or phalloidin treatment also expressed NG2 and their number was significantly higher compared to PFA-fixed retinas (PFA: 509 ± 30 vessels, methanol: 883 ± 56 vessels, phalloidin: 890 ± 138 vessels, p=0.035, ANOVA) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Administration of phalloidin combined with methanol fixation confirmed abundant α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes of the intermediate and deeper retinal plexus.
source: Administration of phalloidin combined with methanol fixation also confirmed abundant α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes of the intermediate (PFA: 97 ± 23 pericytes, methanol: 424 ± 72 pericytes, phalloidin: 509 ± 79 pericytes, jasplakinolide: 497 ± 99 pericytes, p=0.03; ANOVA) and deeper (PFA: 4 ± 2.7 pericytes, methanol: 119 ± 27 pericytes, phalloidin: 260 ± 30 pericytes, jasplakinolide: 359 ± 96 pericytes, p=0.01; ANOVA) retinal plexus (Figures 2A–D and 3C–D, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The vast majority of the α-SMA-positive capillary pericytes could only be visualized after methanol fixation at −20°C or upon in vivo administration of jasplakinolide or phalloidin.
source: The vast majority of the α-SMA-positive capillary pericytes could only be visualized after methanol fixation at −20°C (Figures 2A, C–D and 3C–D; Figure 2—video 1) or upon in vivo administration of jasplakinolide or phalloidin (Figures 1C, 2B, 3A and C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Pericytes at the junction of two capillaries (junctional pericytes) were more frequently α-SMA-positive and exhibited a characteristic circular staining pattern wrapping microvessels.
source: Of interest, we found that pericytes at the junction of two capillaries (i.e. junctional pericytes) were more frequently α-SMA-positive and exhibited a characteristic circular staining pattern wrapping microvessels.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Pericytes on the linear segment of the capillary displayed a helical strand-like staining pattern and were less often α-SMA-positive.
source: In contrast, pericytes on the linear segment of the capillary, which displayed a helical strand-like staining pattern as reported by other groups (Nehls and Drenckhahn, 1991; Hartmann et al., 2015; Sims, 1986), were less often α-SMA-positive.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data, with citations to previous reports of the helical pattern.

claim: α-SMA-siRNA significantly suppressed α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes 48 hr after intravitreal administration.
source: α-SMA-siRNA significantly suppressed α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes 48 hr after intravitreal administration, while α-SMA expression in pericytes on upstream capillary branches and arterioles was less affected (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–F.

claim: α-SMA expression in pericytes on upstream capillary branches and arterioles was less affected by α-SMA-siRNA compared to capillary pericytes.
source: α-SMA-siRNA significantly suppressed α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes 48 hr after intravitreal administration, while α-SMA expression in pericytes on upstream capillary branches and arterioles was less affected (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–F.

claim: A small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is quickly lost by depolymerization, making its histological detection difficult relative to α-SMA-rich pericytes on pre-capillary arterioles and vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: These results are in agreement with the idea that a small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is quickly lost by depolymerization, hence making its histological detection difficult relative to α-SMA-rich pericytes on pre-capillary arterioles and vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the siRNA knockdown results.

claim: About 50% of NG2-positive pericytes on high order retinal capillaries (i.e. >5th) located in the intermediate and deeper retinal vascular plexus express α-SMA.
source: In this report, we demonstrate that about 50% of NG2-positive pericytes on high order retinal capillaries (i.e. >5th) located in the intermediate and deeper retinal vascular plexus express α-SMA (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Previous reports relied on α-SMA immunohistochemistry involving the slow transcardial infusion of formaldehyde or PFA fixatives.
source: Previous reports relied on α-SMA immunohistochemistry involving the slow transcardial infusion of formaldehyde or PFA fixatives (Thavarajah et al., 2012), thus lack of or weak α-SMA detection was likely due to rapid F-actin depolymerization (Huber et al., 2013) leading to the disruption of the antibody-binding sites (Dudnakova et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on fixation methods and F-actin depolymerization.

claim: Lack of or weak α-SMA detection in previous reports was likely due to rapid F-actin depolymerization leading to the disruption of the antibody-binding sites.
source: Previous reports relied on α-SMA immunohistochemistry involving the slow transcardial infusion of formaldehyde or PFA fixatives (Thavarajah et al., 2012), thus lack of or weak α-SMA detection was likely due to rapid F-actin depolymerization (Huber et al., 2013) leading to the disruption of the antibody-binding sites (Dudnakova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to studies on F-actin depolymerization and antibody-binding.

claim: Faster tissue fixation with cold methanol strikingly increased the detection of α-SMA-positive pericytes.
source: Here, we show that faster tissue fixation with cold methanol strikingly increased the detection of α-SMA-positive pericytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The detection of the minute pool of α-SMA in small soma and processes of pericytes might be difficult to visualize in transgenic mice due to dispersion of the limited amount of membrane-bound reporter protein over the relatively large surface area of the pericyte membrane.
source: It is possible that the detection of the minute pool of α-SMA in small soma and processes of pericytes does not only depend on the fixation method, but might also be difficult to visualize in transgenic mice due to dispersion of the limited amount of membrane-bound reporter protein over the relatively large surface area of the pericyte membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for difficulties in detecting α-SMA in transgenic mice.

claim: Incomplete (mosaic-like) fluorescent protein expression after tamoxifen injection in inducible transgenic mice can account for the failure to visualize low levels of α-SMA labeling at capillary pericytes.
source: Moreover, incomplete (mosaic-like) fluorescent protein expression after tamoxifen injection in inducible transgenic mice, in which Cre recombinase expression is driven by the α-SMA promoter, can also account for the failure to visualize low levels of α-SMA labeling at capillary pericytes (Hill et al., 2015; Hartmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by citations to studies on inducible transgenic mice.

claim: Inhibition of α-SMA depolymerization in the intact eye using phalloidin or jasplakinolide substantially increased visualization of α-SMA in retinal capillary pericytes, particularly those in the deeper retinal plexus.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that inhibition of α-SMA depolymerization in the intact eye using phalloidin or jasplakinolide, two F-actin stabilizing reagents with different pharmacological effects on F-actin, substantially increased visualization of α-SMA in retinal capillary pericytes, particularly those in the deeper retinal plexus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The ratio of α-SMA-positive pericytes was relatively lower in distal capillaries compared to upstream microvessels, consistent with previous reports showing less net O2 delivery from distal capillaries relative to proximal ones.
source: The ratio of α-SMA-positive pericytes was relatively lower to that found in upstream microvessels, consistent with previous reports showing less net O2 delivery from distal capillaries relative to proximal ones (Sakadžić et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to a previous study on O2 delivery.

claim: Knocking down α-SMA expression led to the disappearance of α-SMA immunostaining mainly in distal capillary pericytes, suggesting that the small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is less stable than in vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: Interestingly, knocking down α-SMA expression led to the disappearance of α-SMA immunostaining mainly in distal capillary pericytes, suggesting that the small pool of α-SMA in capillary pericytes is less stable than in vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the siRNA knockdown experimental results.

claim: A large population of pericytes, notably those at branching points of retinal microvessels, have the capacity to express α-SMA, which likely mediates their contraction.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that a large population of pericytes, notably those at branching points of retinal microvessels, have the capacity to express α-SMA, which likely mediates their contraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: γ-actin might contribute to pericyte contractility in cortical microvessels according to Grant et al. 2017.
source: It has been suggested that γ-actin might contribute to pericyte contractility in cortical microvessels (Grant et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grant et al. 2017.

claim: The authors' results do not support the hypothesis that γ-actin contributes to pericyte contractility since they did not detect γ-actin-positive capillary pericytes on distal order branches after preventing F-actin depolymerization.
source: However, our results do not support this hypothesis since we did not detect γ-actin-positive capillary pericytes on distal order branches after preventing F-actin depolymerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on γ-actin distribution.

claim: The increase in α-SMA-positivity after phalloidin or jasplakinolide was not caused by cross-reactivity between the antibodies against γ- and α-isoforms or by accumulation of an excess amount of F-actin.
source: The latter finding also indicates that the increase in α-SMA-positivity after phalloidin or jasplakinolide was not caused by cross-reactivity between the antibodies against γ- and α-isoforms or by accumulation of an excess amount of F-actin that might increase the immunostaining of all isoforms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the γ-actin distribution data.

claim: Unlike peripheral tissues where the blood flow changes homogeneously, the density of pericytes is high in the CNS and retina, where the blood flow demand varies considerably between neighboring cell layers or groups.
source: Unlike peripheral tissues where the blood flow changes homogeneously, the density of pericytes is high in the CNS and retina, where the blood flow demand varies considerably between neighboring cell layers or groups (Kornfield and Newman, 2014; Armulik et al., 2011; Schallek et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on pericyte density and blood flow.

claim: In vitro studies and recent in vivo brain studies have provided evidence that capillary pericytes contract or dilate in response to vasoactive mediators.
source: In vitro studies and recent in vivo brain studies have provided a growing body of evidence that capillary pericytes contract or dilate in response to vasoactive mediators (Peppiatt et al., 2006; Fernández-Klett et al., 2010; Puro, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blood flow regulation with fine spatial resolution may be essential for tissues with high functional specialization such as the brain and retina.
source: This blood flow regulation with fine spatial resolution may be essential for tissues with high functional specialization such as the brain and retina.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional importance of pericyte-mediated blood flow regulation.

claim: Retinal capillary dilation in response to light stimulus is layer-specific.
source: The retinal capillary dilation in response to light stimulus is reportedly layer-specific (Kornfield and Newman, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kornfield and Newman 2014.

claim: Kornfield and Newman 2014 reported robust capillary dilation in the intermediate plexus but failed to detect α-SMA expression most likely due to the use of PFA-based fixation.
source: In line with our findings showing clear α-SMA expression in capillary pericytes of the intermediate plexus, the latter study reported robust capillary dilation in this region, but failed to detect α-SMA expression most likely due to the use of PFA-based fixation (Kornfield and Newman, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about why Kornfield and Newman 2014 failed to detect α-SMA, supported by the authors' findings.

claim: A recent study using transgenic mice confirmed the contractile capacity of microvascular pericytes in the cortex in vivo but proposed classifying NG2- and α-SMA-expressing (contractile) cells as smooth muscle cells rather than pericytes.
source: A recent study using transgenic mice expressing fluorescent proteins driven by the NG2 or α-SMA promoters also confirmed the contractile capacity of microvascular pericytes in the cortex in vivo, however, it proposed a radical redefinition by classifying the NG2- and α-SMA-expressing (contractile) cells as smooth muscle cells, rather than pericytes, as they would have conventionally been named under the original Zimmermann definition used since 1923 (Hill et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hill et al. 2015.

claim: The existence of at least three sub-classes of pericytes and transitional forms from smooth muscle cells has been a matter of confusion, emphasizing the need for an unambiguous definition of pericyte sub-classes and their corresponding specialized functions.
source: The existence of at least three sub-classes of pericytes and transitional forms from smooth muscle cells (Zimmermann, 1923) has been a matter of confusion, emphasizing the need for an unambiguous definition of pericyte sub-classes and their corresponding specialized functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by a citation to Zimmermann 1923.

claim: The identification of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may contribute to clarify the current paradox between functional and histological studies.
source: In conclusion, we identify key components of the contractile machinery in a large population of pericytes in the healthy retina. The identification of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may contribute to clarify the current paradox between functional and histological studies, and expand our understanding of the mechanisms regulating blood flow at the single-capillary level in neurodegenerative conditions including stroke, retinal ischemia, diabetic retinopathy and Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the findings.

claim: The identification of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may expand our understanding of the mechanisms regulating blood flow at the single-capillary level in neurodegenerative conditions including stroke, retinal ischemia, diabetic retinopathy and Alzheimer's disease.
source: In conclusion, we identify key components of the contractile machinery in a large population of pericytes in the healthy retina. The identification of α-SMA in capillary pericytes may contribute to clarify the current paradox between functional and histological studies, and expand our understanding of the mechanisms regulating blood flow at the single-capillary level in neurodegenerative conditions including stroke, retinal ischemia, diabetic retinopathy and Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the findings.

claim: Seventy three Swiss albino mice and eleven NG2-DsRed mice were used in the study.
source: Seventy three Swiss albino (21–35 g), eleven NG2-DsRed (Schallek et al., 2013) mice were housed under diurnal lighting conditions (12 hr darkness and 12 hr light) and fed ad libitum.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The inhibition trend of α-SMA by siRNA being more prominent on high order branches was statistically significant (p=0.005) with non-parametric Jonckheere-terpstra test for trend analysis.
source: (C) Illustrates the ratio of microvessels with intact α-SMA immunolabeling in α-SMA-siRNA injected retinas to scrambled (control) siRNA-injected retinas (n = 3 per group). The inhibition trend being more prominent on high order branches was statistically significant (p=0.005) with non-parametric Jonckheere-terpstra test for trend analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Western blotting and qRT-PCR show that both α-SMA protein and α-SMA-mRNA levels were reduced in α-SMA-siRNA injected retinas but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
source: (D–F) Western blotting (D–E) (scrambled-siRNA, n = 3, 1.22 ± 0.32 a.u.; α-SMA-siRNA, n = 3, 0.93 ± 0.23 a.u., p=0.4; Student's t-test) and qRT-PCR (F) (scrambled-siRNA, n = 3, 1.51 ± 0.33 a.u.; α-SMA-siRNA, n = 3, 1.14 ± 0.32 a.u., p=0.7; Student's t-test) show that both α-SMA protein and α-SMA-mRNA levels were reduced in α-SMA-siRNA injected retinas but the difference did not reach statistical significance possibly because the large amounts of α-SMA in proximal microvessels masked the inhibition in high order branches with small pools of α-SMA.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: The large amounts of α-SMA in proximal microvessels possibly masked the inhibition in high order branches with small pools of α-SMA in Western blot and qRT-PCR analyses.
source: (D–F) Western blotting (D–E) (scrambled-siRNA, n = 3, 1.22 ± 0.32 a.u.; α-SMA-siRNA, n = 3, 0.93 ± 0.23 a.u., p=0.4; Student's t-test) and qRT-PCR (F) (scrambled-siRNA, n = 3, 1.51 ± 0.33 a.u.; α-SMA-siRNA, n = 3, 1.14 ± 0.32 a.u., p=0.7; Student's t-test) show that both α-SMA protein and α-SMA-mRNA levels were reduced in α-SMA-siRNA injected retinas but the difference did not reach statistical significance possibly because the large amounts of α-SMA in proximal microvessels masked the inhibition in high order branches with small pools of α-SMA.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of statistical significance in Western blot and qRT-PCR results.
